doc.title: Jane Monheit interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, August 20, 2010

title: Samba, tempos and respecting lyrics and composers
summary: Samba makes everything better; she dislikes arrangements that contradict the lyrics or composer's intent.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: You said an interesting thing about bossa nova music and samba music that I enjoyed. I think you said samba makes everything happy.
It makes everything better. It does. It’s healing music. It is. I think so.
So if you take a tune that’s normally done as a swing tune and make it into a samba — but you also said you mostly dislike changing tempos or feels for songs. I’m not sure I understood.

Well what I mean by that is that generally I don’t like to get too super far away from the composer’s original intention because those guys were brilliant, and mostly what I mean by it is when the lyrics are not taken into account. That drives me batty.

Yeah. And it happens constantly on instrumental versions of tunes, and in that case it’s all right because we’re not hearing the lyrics. But when you say — I don’t know I don’t want to name any examples but I’ve got plenty of them in my head of times when there have been like vocal versions of things where you know the lyrics said a certain thing and the arrangement said another. And I can understand interpreting the lyric in a different way and finding a different meaning in the tune, but when the two are just totally divergent I can’t stand it.
Yeah. Well you’re getting back to what’s right for the music.
And I mean do you care — like if Richard Rogers wanted something to be a certain way, who are you to say that it shouldn’t be?
